import importlib.util
for name in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','pypdfium2']:
    spec=importlib.util.find_spec(name)
    print(name, spec.origin if spec else None)
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
reader=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
out=Path('tmp/pdfs')
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
print('PAGES',len(reader.pages))
texts=[]
for n,page in enumerate(reader.pages,1):
    text=page.extract_text()
    texts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {n} =====\\n\\n{text}')
(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts)[:33000])
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a concrete clinical NLP need: accessible training data for extracting social and behavioral determinants of health. Synth-SBDH offers broader annotation coverage than the compared public resources, including spans, presence, temporality, and rationales. Its principal contribution is a useful dataset and empirical validation.

The evaluation goes beyond synthetic test performance. Experiments use real clinical data from two healthcare settings, multiple model architectures, classification and span extraction, and both exact and relaxed matching. Reporting means and standard deviations over three runs strengthens the evidence.

The classification improvements are substantial for several models. Prompt-based RoBERTa improves from 56.17 to 91.20 macro-F, and ClinicalRoBERTa from 65.90 to 91.13. The category-level results and training-size ablations provide useful evidence that synthetic pretraining can help when labeled examples are scarce.

Expert review of all 1,755 synthetic test examples, explicit correction and addition counts, and qualitative error analysis are valuable investments in resource assessment. The generation prompts, 45 seed examples, category definitions, label mappings, training configurations, and stated public release support reuse. Together with the downstream results, these support a Findings recommendation.
weaknesses: The benchmark-quality claim needs stronger qualification. Experts corrected 286 original annotations, discarded 142, and added 581 missing annotations; the training annotations remain uncorrected. Human agreement is 77.80% even with relaxed span matching, and disagreement adjudication is not described. Appendix D.1 also permits different category choices depending on whether an annotation originated with GPT-4 or was added by an expert. A uniform annotation policy and an independent audit would strengthen confidence in the test set. Some inference rules, such as treating a pension as evidence of financial security, also need clearer justification.

The agreement measures are not directly comparable. The reported 71.06% human–LLM alignment is 2,478 retained annotations divided by 3,487 annotations including human additions. Appendix D.4 states that the LLM evaluation does not identify missing annotations. Consequently, its 90.78% alignment measures a different operation; retention among the original annotations is 85.27%. Explicit denominators and separate span, category, presence, and temporal agreement would make the quality assessment more interpretable.

The largest gains should be contextualized. The 62.36% improvement is relative, corresponding to 35.03 macro-F points for a comparatively weak baseline. Standard ClinicalMamba does not improve, and the best classification result exceeds the best unaugmented result by 1.36 points. The striking housing-insecurity result uses only 18 positive test examples. On VA-SBDH, the strongest encoder's exact macro-F increases only from 70.21 to 70.43. Run-to-run standard deviations do not establish test-sample uncertainty or justify blanket claims of significant, consistent improvement.

The controls establish the usefulness of the additional synthetic-training procedure, but do not isolate why it helps. Comparisons with class rebalancing, oversampling, another synthetic-data source, or additional baseline training are absent. This matters because synthetic pretraining adds substantial optimization, and Figure 2 shows smaller benefits when downstream training lasts longer. Claims about compute efficiency should account for the extra pretraining cost.

The demonstrated scope is narrower than some generalizability and distillation claims. Synthetic examples average 13.7 words, substantially shorter than the real datasets, and all real-data evaluations include target-domain fine-tuning. These results establish useful initialization rather than direct transfer to an unseen hospital. The experiments retain only presence-positive annotations and do not evaluate temporal prediction. Rationale distillation is tested only on synthetic text, with gains of 0.66 and 0.58 macro-F points; this is preliminary evidence for auxiliary supervision, not demonstrated transfer of reasoning capability.

Some reproducibility and reporting details remain incomplete. The manuscript omits the exact prompt-based classification templates and verbalizers, although these produce the headline results, and generation sampling settings are unspecified. VA-SBDH is private, limiting independent replication of the NER findings. The reported synthetic split sizes also sum to 8,727 rather than 8,767. These gaps should be corrected. Overall, the evidence supports a useful training resource more convincingly than a broadly validated benchmark, limiting the case for main-conference publication.
